questions.explain: SQL Server licensing bills a four-vCPU minimum per instance, so downsizing 4→2 vCPU saves ~$200/month in compute but $0 in licensing; the moves that cross the licensing floor are 8→4 (with SMT disabled) or edition changes.
options: The four-vCPU licensing floor means downsizing 4→2 vCPU saves compute but zero licensing dollars
Licensing is billed on provisioned storage, not vCPUs
The floor only applies to Express edition
There is no minimum; licensing scales linearly from 1 vCPU

questions.explain: Enterprise ($0.47) → Standard ($0.13) cuts the licensing line by 72% ($2,745 → $759/month on 8 vCPU); the chapter says to audit every instance against actual Enterprise feature usage and downgrade where eligible.

Express → Standard, the only supported downgrade path
Enterprise → Web, which is always eligible
Enterprise ($0.47/core-hour) → Standard ($0.13) cuts the licensing line by 72% for workloads not using Enterprise-only features

questions.explain: CUDs discount vCPU and memory only (25% for 1 year, up to 52% for 3 years) — never the licensing line, which is 65–80% of the bill — so a headline 52% discount is roughly 10–15% of the total bill; also, commit only after right-sizing to the validated baseline.
options: CUDs apply to licensing too, making 3-year commitments always the best deal
CUDs discount compute only — not the 65–80% licensing line — so model ROI against compute-only spend and commit only after right-sizing
CUDs are instance-based and cannot cover multiple instances
CUDs require the Enterprise edition
